summary: Defines the Minimal Scheduling Function for 6TiSCH, covering what a node does when joining and how the communication schedule is managed in a distributed way. It builds on the 6P sublayer protocol and the minimal security framework.

eli5.summary: Each little sensor decides when it talks and listens, adjusting its schedule as traffic changes, without a central boss.

questions: how does msf manage tsch schedules
what is the 6tisch minimal scheduling function
what is an autonomous cell in tsch
how does msf add and delete cells
subtitle: The default rules a 6TiSCH node follows to join a network and to add, remove and move its radio time slots.

tldr.problem: In a TSCH network, a schedule says when each node transmits or receives on which channel. Someone has to decide when nodes add or remove cells, and what a new node does at boot.
tldr.mechanism: MSF builds on 6P, the minimal 6TiSCH configuration and the Constrained Join Protocol. Nodes use hash-derived autonomous cells for joining, then negotiate cells with their RPL parent, adding or deleting them by watching how many are used.
tldr.outcome: The schedule is managed in a distributed fashion with no central scheduler. MSF defines no new protocol or packet format, and its autonomous cells can be targeted by selective jamming because they are computed from visible EUI-64 addresses.

today: RFC 9033 is a Proposed Standard from May 2021 and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It sits on top of RFC 8480 and the join protocol in RFC 9031.

sections.title: What MSF Is
sections.content:
The Minimal Scheduling Function (MSF) is a 6TiSCH Scheduling Function (SF). The role of an SF is defined in RFC 8480; MSF adds the rules of when to add and delete cells in the communication schedule. It builds on the minimal 6TiSCH configuration (RFC 8180), the 6top protocol 6P (RFC 8480) and the Constrained Join Protocol (RFC 9031).

MSF defines both what a node does when it boots and how the schedule is managed afterwards. It works with the RPL routing parent, called the selected parent, and is optimized for applications with regular upstream traffic towards the DODAG root.
sections.eli5: MSF is the rulebook that says how a sensor picks its talking and listening times, and how it changes them later.

sections.title: Slotframes, Cells and Autonomous Cells
sections.content:
TSCH divides time into slots grouped into slotframes that repeat. A cell is a (slot, channel) pair. MSF uses three slotframes: Slotframe 0 for bootstrap traffic as in the minimal 6TiSCH configuration, Slotframe 1 for autonomous cells, and Slotframe 2 for cells negotiated through 6P. The same length is RECOMMENDED for all three. The minimal cell carries broadcasts such as EBs and DIOs, and cells scheduled by MSF are for unicast frames only. Broadcast traffic SHOULD NOT exceed one-third of the minimal cell's bandwidth.

Autonomous cells need no negotiation. The AutoRxCell is computed as a hash of the node's own EUI-64 and always stays scheduled. The AutoTxCell is computed from the destination's EUI-64 and is added only when a frame must be sent and no negotiated Tx cell exists. Nodes MUST use the SAX hash function; the slot offset is 1 + hash(EUI64, length(Slotframe_1) - 1), so the first slot, used by the minimal cell, is skipped.
sections.eli5: Every sensor has a mailbox at a time and place worked out from its serial number, so anyone who knows the number knows where to knock.

sections.title: Node Behavior at Boot
sections.content:
A booting node follows six steps. In step 1 the pledge randomly picks a frequency and listens for EBs. In step 2 it keeps listening for additional EBs, for at most MAX_EB_DELAY seconds or until it has heard NUM_NEIGHBOURS_TO_WAIT distinct neighbors, and chooses a Join Proxy. It may filter EBs by PANID, by the IE defined in RFC 9032, or by the authentication key.

In step 3 the pledge installs an AutoTxCell to the Join Proxy and sends its Join Request. The proxy forwards it to the Join Registrar/Coordinator, and the Join Response comes back over an AutoTxCell, giving the keying material. In step 4 the joined node receives DIOs, computes its Rank and selects a routing parent. In step 5 it MUST send a 6P ADD Request through an AutoTxCell with CellOptions TX=1, RX=0, SHARED=0, NumCells set to 1 and a CellList of at least 5 cells, repeating until a Tx cell is installed. In step 6 it starts sending EBs and DIOs on the minimal cell.

At the end the node is synchronized, uses the link-layer keys it learned, has one AutoRxCell, one negotiated Tx cell to its parent, and may serve as a router and Join Proxy.
sections.eli5: A new sensor listens for a friendly neighbor, gets its password through that neighbor, picks a boss, asks for one regular time slot, and then starts helping others.

sections.title: Adding, Deleting and Moving Cells
sections.content:
After joining, a node changes cells for three reasons: to match traffic, to switch parent, and to fix schedule collisions. To match traffic, it keeps two counters per direction for its parent: NumCellsElapsed counts negotiated cells that have passed, and NumCellsUsed counts those where a frame was sent or a valid frame received. When NumCellsElapsed reaches MAX_NUM_CELLS, a node adds one cell if NumCellsUsed is above LIM_NUMCELLSUSED_HIGH and removes one if it is below LIM_NUMCELLSUSED_LOW, then resets both counters.

When switching parent, the node counts its negotiated cells to the old parent, uses 6P ADD to schedule the same number to the new one, and then sends 6P CLEAR to the old one.

For collisions, the node counts NumTx and NumTxAck per negotiated Tx cell and computes the Packet Delivery Ratio. Every HOUSEKEEPINGCOLLISION_PERIOD it compares each cell to the best one; if a cell is worse by more than RELOCATE_PDRTHRES, it triggers a 6P RELOCATE. Relocation of negotiated Rx cells is not supported.
sections.eli5: If your slots are mostly full you ask for another, and if they are mostly empty you give one back. If one slot keeps losing messages, you move it.

sections.title: CellList Rules, Error Handling and Constants
sections.content:
MSF uses two-step 6P transactions only, always started by a node towards its parent. A CellList is RECOMMENDED to have five or more cells. Each cell MUST have a different slotOffset, MUST NOT share a slotOffset with any cell the node already has, and MUST NOT use slotOffset 0 (the minimal cell). Offsets SHOULD be chosen randomly and uniformly. The 6P SIGNAL command and the Metadata field are not used, and the SFID of MSF is 0.

For 6P errors, RC_SUCCESS and RC_EOL need nothing. RC_ERR, RC_RESET, RC_ERR_VERSION and RC_ERR_SFID call for quarantine: do what clear does, drop the node from the neighbor and routing tables and ignore its frames for QUARANTINE_DURATION. RC_ERR_SEQNUM and RC_ERR_CELLLIST call for clear, which aborts the transaction, sends 6P CLEAR and removes all cells with that neighbor. RC_ERR_BUSY and RC_ERR_LOCKED call for waitretry: wait a random time between WAIT_DURATION_MIN and WAIT_DURATION_MAX and retry.
sections.eli5: When a request goes wrong, the sensor either starts over with that neighbor, stops trusting it for a while, or waits a bit and tries again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
MSF defines no new protocol or packet format, so the security of its traffic comes from RFC 8180, RFC 8480 and RFC 9031. Autonomous cells are a hash of EUI-64 addresses, which are visible on the wire and not encrypted at the link layer. An attacker can therefore selectively jam a node's AutoRxCell. If the target is a Join Proxy, pledges can pseudorandomly pick another one. If the target is a particular pledge, the RFC says this should be detected by the node's absence and handled by the administrator out of band.

Join traffic from unauthenticated pledges may carry a nonzero DSCP, and the IPv6 layer SHOULD rate limit it before it reaches the 6top sublayer, to avoid resource exhaustion.
sections.eli5: Since anyone can work out where a sensor listens, a bad actor could shout over that spot. Having several helpers to try is the defense.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA added SFID 0, named Minimal Scheduling Function (MSF), to the "6P Scheduling Function Identifiers" subregistry defined by RFC 8480. It came from the range 0-127, which uses IETF Review or IESG Approval.
sections.eli5: MSF got number zero in the official list of scheduling rulebooks.
